entry.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

link.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

entry.content:
Every PyTorch practitioner eventually hits the same wall: the training loop that ran beautifully on a laptop needs distributed ranks, gradient synchronization, loss scaling, and device juggling the moment it meets real hardware, and the boilerplate for all of that dwarfs the actual science. huggingface/accelerate, the Apache-2.0 library under most modern Hugging Face training stacks, takes a different path from the monolithic trainer frameworks: it refuses to own your loop. You keep writing the while-loop you already understand, add five lines, and the same script runs on one CPU, eight GPUs, a TPU pod, or any of a growing zoo of accelerators, with fp8, fp16, or bf16 mixed precision handled underneath. The library is deliberately thin in philosophy and decidedly not thin in engineering, which is exactly what makes its source worth reading. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository splits cleanly into four layers. The command-line layer gives you accelerate config, a questionnaire that saves your hardware setup, and accelerate launch, a 1338-line launcher that knows how to start single or multi-node runs without you memorizing torch.distributed.run flags. The state layer, state.py at 1181 lines, holds three singletons that discover the environment once and share it everywhere. The core layer is accelerator.py, 3738 lines around a single Accelerator class whose prepare method wraps whatever you hand it. And the device layer is a hook system: AlignDevicesHook and its offloading cousins move pieces of models between CPU, disk, and accelerator memory at execution time, the machinery that lets Transformers load a 30B model on a single consumer card. Reading the overview from left to right traces a request from the terminal, through environment detection, into the core, and down into the hooks that physically move tensors.

Overview of Accelerate: the CLI launches scripts that read shared state singletons, the Accelerator wraps training objects in one call, and the hook system performs device placement and offloading.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • accelerate config is a 70-line command that walks you through hardware questions and writes a reusable default_config.yaml.
  • accelerate launch is the 1338-line CLI that translates that config into worker processes, env vars, and backend-specific arguments.
  • launchers.py is the 285-line fallback that starts distributed runs from inside a plain script or notebook when no launcher process exists.
  • state.py is the source of truth: PartialState at line 123, AcceleratorState at 877, and GradientState at 1240 resolve the environment exactly once per process.
  • Accelerator is the class at line 184 that your script imports, holding prepare, backward, logging, and checkpoint methods.
  • prepare is the one call, at line 1414, that adapts a model, data loaders, optimizer, and scheduler to the current setup.
  • hooks.py is the placement engine, from the 58-line ModelHook base to AlignDevicesHook at line 242 and CpuOffload at 721.
  • big_modeling.py is the public toolkit for huge weights: init_empty_weights, cpu_offload, disk_offload, and dispatch_model.

Why You Need This

The README sells the library with a diff, and the diff is honest. You add the import, construct an Accelerator, replace the device literal with accelerator.device, wrap your model, optimizer, and dataloader in prepare, and swap loss.backward for accelerator.backward. Five edited lines. The same file then runs unchanged on a single GPU, a multi-GPU node, or a TPU, with mixed precision selected by config instead of code edits. A second variant in the README goes further: hand device placement to the library entirely and delete the to(device) calls, letting prepare move data and modules for you. This is a genuinely different contract from trainer frameworks; nothing is taken away, which is why so many projects adopt it incrementally rather than as a rewrite.

The hardware coverage in state.py is the part outsiders underestimate. The detection logic recognizes MULTI_GPU and XLA, of course, but also MULTI_MLU, MULTI_SDAA, MULTI_MUSA, MULTI_NPU, MULTI_HPU, MULTI_XPU, and MULTI_NEURON, falling back to MULTI_CPU or plain NO when nothing exotic is present. That list is the footprint of real-world inference and training hardware across vendors, and Accelerate is one of the few libraries that normalizes all of it behind one Accelerator object. Your loop never learns which accelerator it is on; the state singletons do, once, at import time, through a thread-local store that keeps parallel test runs from colliding.

The third reason is the big-model side, which has quietly become infrastructure for the entire ecosystem. init_empty_weights at line 62 of big_modeling.py builds a model on the meta device so a 70B parameter architecture costs kilobytes of RAM until weights arrive. dispatch_model at line 315 then assigns each layer to a device, and load_checkpoint_and_dispatch at line 524 streams the checkpoint in and wires it up. The CpuOffload hook, at line 721 of hooks.py, streams weights to the accelerator just before each forward and discards them after, trading a little latency for a lot of memory. If you have ever loaded a model larger than your GPU, you have run this code path.

Detail view: the launch commands, every major Accelerator method with its line number, the three state singletons and the device enum, the hook classes, and the big-model plus wrapper utilities.

The state layer rewards a close look because everything else leans on it. PartialState, at line 123 of state.py, is usable in any script with or without the Accelerator: it reads the environment variables that a launcher exported, queries the process group, and exposes device and distributed_type. AcceleratorState, at line 877, is the shared instance that all Accelerator objects in one process agree on, which is how a notebook can construct two Accelerators without starting two process groups. GradientState, at line 1240, is the smallest and most subtle: it tracks whether the current micro-batch is inside a no_sync window so that gradient accumulation skips process-group reductions on all but the last step. The AcceleratedOptimizer wrapper in optimizer.py, at line 38, consults that state before letting a step through, which is how accumulation works without touching your loop.

prepare itself is a dispatcher with seventeen special cases. The model path, prepare_model at line 1769, casts dtypes, attaches hooks, and handles compile and quantization integration; prepare_data_loader at line 2684 builds a DataLoaderShard whose BatchSamplerShard, at line 110 of data_loader.py, splits batches evenly and pads uneven tails so ranks never hang waiting for a straggler batch; prepare_optimizer and prepare_scheduler, at lines 2743 and 2787, wrap into the gated AcceleratedOptimizer and AcceleratedScheduler at line 25 of scheduler.py. The 1295-line data_loader.py module also contributes SeedableRandomSampler at line 73, which makes random data order reproducible across ranks, and DataLoaderDispatcher at line 726 for setups where the data loader lives on one process and steps happen elsewhere.

The backward path is where precision engineering hides. accelerator.backward at line 2828 routes through the native accelerator scaler for fp16, the native bf16 path, or fp8 handling depending on configuration, then calls the underlying loss.backward with the right arguments. clip_grad_norm_ at line 2988 knows to unscale gradients before measuring norms, a detail many hand-rolled loops get wrong. On the metrics side, gather_for_metrics at line 3108 collects tensors from every rank and drops the padding that the even-batch sharding introduced, so your accuracy numbers are computed on real samples only. save_state at line 3624 and load_state at 3790 round-trip the entire setup, model, optimizer, schedulers, random states, and registration order included, which is what makes interrupted distributed runs resumable at all.

The hook system is the architectural trick that keeps all of this composable. ModelHook at line 58 of hooks.py is a tiny class that wraps a module’s forward and detach; add_hook_to_module at line 147 attaches one to any nn.Module by overriding its forward, and SequentialHook at 116 chains them. AlignDevicesHook at line 242 is the workhorse: on entry it casts and moves a module’s parameters and buffers to its execution device, runs the wrapped forward, and optionally offloads again on exit. attach_align_device_hook_on_blocks at line 587 applies it recursively to every block of a model, which is precisely how dispatch_model implements its device map. The 742-line big_modeling.py module is just the public face of this machinery, and utils/modeling.py, at 1942 lines, supplies the weight-loading and offload-store utilities underneath, while utils/operations.py, at 808 lines, converts tensor sends, pads, and reductions into their distributed equivalents.

From Install to a Launched Run

Configure once, then launch:

pip install accelerate

accelerate config          # answer questions about GPU count, precision, distributed setup
accelerate launch train.py # starts single or multi-GPU training with zero code flags

Inside train.py, the whole integration is the five-line diff from the README:

# from accelerate import Accelerator
# accelerator = Accelerator()
# device = accelerator.device
# model, optimizer, data = accelerator.prepare(model, optimizer, data)
# accelerator.backward(loss)

The first two commands pick up default_config.yaml written by the questionnaire, so teammates and CI machines share one launch recipe instead of a wiki page of torchrun flags.

Honest limits: Accelerate deliberately does not schedule training for you, so learning-rate policy, evaluation cadence, and checkpoint rotation remain your loop’s job, and projects that want those managed graduate to Trainer or TRL on top. The five-line promise holds for standard loops, but exotic patterns such as two optimizers with different accumulation schedules or hand-written process-group collectives still leak distributed concepts through the abstraction. The hook-based offloading trades latency for memory and is tuned for inference-shaped workloads, not every training shape. And the device zoo, impressive as the enum is, means the long tail of accelerators gets community-tested coverage rather than vendor-certified support. What the source shows, line after line, is an unusual discipline: a library that grew to underpin an ecosystem while refusing to take your training loop hostage.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/accelerate: how one 3738-line Accelerator class, three state singletons, and a hook system for device placement turn a raw PyTorch training loop into multi-GPU, TPU, and mixed-precision code.

entry.title: Train 0.19 Percent of the Model - Inside huggingface/peft

link.title: Train 0.19 Percent of the Model - Inside huggingface/peft

entry.content:
Full fine-tuning is the luxury the rest of us cannot afford. A 12B-parameter model in fp16 needs around 47GB of GPU memory before the optimizer even gets its share, which is why so many promising fine-tuning projects died the moment someone loaded the weights. huggingface/peft, the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning library, is the industry’s standard answer: freeze the backbone, learn a tiny set of extra weights instead, and ship checkpoints measured in megabytes. The Apache-2.0 repository has grown into a zoo of 46 tuner methods, from LoRA and DoRA through prompt tuning, IA3, VeRA, and X-LoRA, all sharing one injection framework and one checkpoint format. It is the library underneath QLoRA training jobs, TRL reinforcement-learning runs, and countless adapter swaps on the Hub. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The codebase is organized with unusual discipline for something this dynamic. The public entry point is a single function, get_peft_model, in an 81-line dispatch module that maps a config object to a tuner class through registries that methods register themselves into. The wrapper layer, peft_model.py, runs 3242 lines and adds six task-specific subclasses on top of the base PeftModel. Underneath, every tuner follows the same contract defined in tuners_utils.py: walk the model, find target modules, replace them with wrapped layers. The LoRA implementation is the reference citizen, with a 2429-line layer file that carries the full math of low-rank adaptation, including rank-stabilized scaling, per-layer rank patterns, DoRA magnitude vectors, and merge and unmerge surgery on quantized weights. Reading the overview from left to right shows a clean funnel: two entry functions, a registry, one big wrapper family, and one tuner contract.

Overview of PEFT: two entry functions share a registry of tuner classes, PeftModel and its six task subclasses wrap the result, and the LoRA tuner demonstrates the layer contract that all 46 methods follow.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • get_peft_model is the front door: it resolves a config such as LoraConfig into a tuner, injects the adapters, and hands back a PeftModel.
  • inject_adapter_in_model is the lower-level sibling that mutates your model in place and returns the same object, for people who already have their own wrapper.
  • register_peft_method is how the 46 methods plug in: each tuner registers its config class, tuner class, and checkpoint prefix into shared tables.
  • PeftModel is the base wrapper at line 140, carrying adapter add, load, set, and delete operations plus save_pretrained and generate.
  • six task subclasses specialize forward and generate for causal LM, seq2seq, classification, token classification, question answering, and feature extraction.
  • LoraModel is the reference tuner: it walks named_modules and swaps every target for a LoRA-wrapped copy, honoring per-key rank and alpha patterns.
  • LoraLayer holds the math: per-adapter rank, the A and B matrices, the alpha-over-r scaling, and the merge code that folds adapters into base weights.
  • save_and_load.py is why checkpoints stay tiny: it filters the state dict down to adapter weights only, keyed by adapter name.

Why You Need This

The README opens with a table that explains the entire value proposition in three rows. On an A100 80GB GPU, full fine-tuning of bigscience/T0_3B consumes 47.14GB of GPU memory; the same model with LoRA needs 14.4GB; LoRA plus DeepSpeed CPU offloading brings it to 9.8GB. Move up to the 12B mt0-xxl and full fine-tuning runs out of memory entirely, while LoRA fits at 56GB and offloaded LoRA at 22GB. The bloomz-7b1 numbers follow the same shape. Quality holds up too: on the twitter_complaints task, the LoRA-trained T0 scores 0.863 against a Flan-T5 baseline of 0.892 and a crowdsourced human baseline of 0.897.

Storage is the second argument, and it is the one that changed how people share models. A full T0_3B checkpoint is 11GB; the LoRA adapter for the same model is 19MB, roughly a 500-fold reduction. That ratio is what makes the adapter economy on the Hugging Face Hub possible: one frozen backbone on disk, hundreds of task adapters beside it, each a few megabytes. The library leans into this with load_adapter and set_adapter on PeftModel, so a serving process can hot-swap personalities without reloading weights, and with create_or_update_model_card, which writes a metadata card into every checkpoint folder it saves.

The third argument is the quantization story that became QLoRA. The LoRA tuner ships dedicated wrapper files for bitsandbytes 4-bit and 8-bit layers, plus GPTQ, AQLM, AWQ, HQQ, and EETQ formats, each teaching the adapter how to dequantize, add the low-rank update, and merge back without ever materializing the full fp16 weight. The README points to a recipe that fine-tunes meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf on a 16GB consumer GPU using exactly this path. If you have ever wondered what actually happens between “load_in_4bit” and a trainable layer, this is the code that answers it.

Detail view: the entry and registry layer, the PeftModel family with its adapter lifecycle, the LoRA internals from config to scaling to merge, and the quantized variants plus checkpoint format.

Start at the entry points. get_peft_model, defined at line 105 of mapping_func.py, and inject_adapter_in_model, at line 47 of mapping.py, both depend on tables that start empty: PEFT_TYPE_TO_CONFIG_MAPPING, PEFT_TYPE_TO_TUNER_MAPPING, and friends are dicts in mapping.py that register_peft_method fills at import time. That registration pattern is why the library can carry 46 methods without a single if-chain in its dispatch code; adding a tuner means adding a folder and a registration call, never touching the front door. The injection function does enforce a few hard rules, rejecting prompt-learning methods and tuners with shared state, since those need the full PeftModel wrapper rather than bare mutation.

PeftModel, at line 140 of peft_model.py, is where the wrapper personality lives. Its constructor branches on whether the config is prompt-learning: prompt methods keep the raw model and hang a prompt encoder off it, while everything else instantiates the tuner class from the registry, which returns the model with wrapped layers inside. After wrapping it casts adapter dtypes, prepares gradient checkpointing, and forces pretraining_tp to 1 to avoid numerical surprises from tensor-simulation settings. The adapter lifecycle is explicit and worth knowing for serving: add_adapter at line 1109, load_adapter at 1515, set_adapter at 1705, and delete_adapter at 1190. Meanwhile get_nb_trainable_parameters at line 953 powers print_trainable_parameters, the call that prints the famous line from the README quickstart: 3,686,400 trainable parameters out of 3,089,625,088 total, or 0.1193 percent, for a Qwen2.5-3B model with rank 16.

The LoRA internals repay a slow read. LoraLayer, at line 108 of layer.py, keeps per-adapter dicts of rank, the A and B matrices, dropout, and scaling, so multiple adapters coexist in one layer. In update_layer, lora_A is created as a plain nn.Linear from in_features down to rank r, and lora_B as an nn.Linear from r back up to out_features; A gets kaiming-uniform initialization while B starts at zero, which is the trick that keeps the initial adapter output silent. The scaling factor is lora_alpha divided by r at line 281, or alpha over the square root of r when use_rslora is set, following the rank-stabilized recipe. Forward passes then compute base_layer(x) plus the scaled B-times-A projection, and the merge code computes the delta weight as exactly that product so adapters can be folded into the base matrix and later unfolded without loss.

The traversal side is LoraModel, at line 165 of model.py. Its _create_and_replace at line 294 resolves per-key overrides first: rank_pattern and alpha_pattern are dicts of regex-to-value, looked up with get_pattern_key against the current module name, so you can ask for rank 64 on attention projections and rank 8 everywhere else in one config. It then passes r, alpha, and quantization flags into _create_new_module at line 499, which picks the right wrapper class for the target, including the quantized variants. If the target is already a LoRA layer, it simply adds another adapter to it, which is how multi-adapter layers work. The config file itself is a study in accretion: LoraConfig at line 514 is surrounded by companion configs for runtime options, VeRA, LoftQ, ARROW, EVA, CorDA, and more, each representing a research refinement the community adopted.

Persistence is the quiet achievement. get_peft_model_state_dict at line 148 of save_and_load.py extracts only adapter weights, remaps their names into the checkpoint format, and set_peft_model_state_dict at line 549 reverses the process on load, with load_peft_weights at 702 handling the remote fetch from the Hub. The artifact is two files, adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json, the name defined in constants.py at line 400. Because every method uses the same keys, a checkpoint carries its own config and can be loaded years later without the original training script. For debugging, TunerLayerStatus and TunerModelStatus at lines 3358 and 3488 print per-layer tables of what is wrapped where, and mixed_model.py, at 397 lines, composes several methods into one model for the rare cases where LoRA plus prompt tuning is genuinely the answer.

From Install to a Trained Adapter

The quickstart from the README trains a rank-16 LoRA adapter on a 3B model in a few lines:

pip install peft

python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from peft import LoraConfig, TaskType, get_peft_model

device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator().type if hasattr(torch, "accelerator") else "cuda"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct", device_map=device)
peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM)
model = get_peft_model(model, peft_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# trainable params: 3,686,400 || all params: 3,089,625,088 || trainable%: 0.1193

# train with your favorite Trainer, then:
model.save_pretrained("qwen2.5-3b-lora")
PY

Loading for inference mirrors it: rebuild the base model, then PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, “qwen2.5-3b-lora”) reattaches the adapter and you can generate immediately.

Honest limits: PEFT is a wrapper library, not a trainer, so you still bring Transformers, Accelerate, or TRL for the training loop, and the README’s own examples lean on those siblings for scheduling and distributed setup. Prompt-learning methods and tuners with shared state cannot use the in-place injection API, a restriction the code states rather than hides. The 46-method zoo is a strength and a hazard: method quality varies by task and model, and the README is candid that numbers like the 0.863 accuracy come from an unoptimized configuration you can probably beat with tuning. Merging adapters into base weights is lossless only when you control the dtype math, and on quantized backbones the merge path is necessarily heavier. None of that diminishes the core result this repository proves line by line: for a very large class of adaptation problems, the 99.88 percent of the model you were about to train did not need training at all.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/peft: how 46 adapter methods, a 3242-line PeftModel shell, and per-layer LoRA scaling math let you fine-tune a 3B-parameter LLM by training less than one percent of its weights.

entry.title: The Engine That Sharded BLOOM - Inside microsoft/DeepSpeed

link.title: The Engine That Sharded BLOOM - Inside microsoft/DeepSpeed

entry.content:
When Microsoft’s AI at Scale initiative committed to training language models measured in hundreds of billions of parameters, the binding constraint was not model design but memory arithmetic. A 176-billion-parameter model in mixed precision needs hundreds of gigabytes just to hold its weights, and several times more once optimizer states and gradients join the party. DeepSpeed is the open-source training system Microsoft built to break that wall, and its track record is written into the repository’s own README: Megatron-Turing NLG at 530 billion parameters, BLOOM at 176 billion, Jurassic-1 at 178 billion, YaLM at 100 billion, GPT-NeoX at 20 billion, and Turing NLG at 17 billion all passed through this engine. The whole system ships under the Apache 2.0 license, which means every trick that made those runs fit is sitting in plain sight in the source tree.

What surprises first-time readers is how much of the system lives in plain Python. Beneath a thin layer of fused CUDA kernels, DeepSpeed is an orchestrator: a launcher that SSHes into your cluster, an engine class that re-implements the training loop with sharded bookkeeping, three ZeRO stages that progressively cut memory, a pipe-parallel subsystem, an autotuner, and a hardware abstraction that now speaks NVIDIA, AMD, Ascend, Gaudi, Intel XPU, and plain CPU. Reading it teaches you how modern distributed training actually works, one hook and one partition at a time. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

DeepSpeed overview: two entry points feed the DeepSpeedEngine, which drives the ZeRO stages, pipe and MoE parallelism, and a platform layer of collectives, accelerator backends, and JIT-compiled ops.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • the initialize() entry point — one call that wraps a plain PyTorch model and a JSON config into a managed distributed engine.
  • the launcher runner — parses a hostfile into a resource pool and fans out training processes across machines over SSH.
  • DeepSpeedEngine — the 5,153-line heart of the library where forward, backward, and step acquire their distributed meaning.
  • ZeRO stage 1 and 2 — partitions optimizer states and gradients across data-parallel ranks.
  • ZeRO stage 3 — shards the parameters themselves, with CPU and NVMe offload in the ZeRO-Infinity style.
  • partition_parameters.py — the zero.Init machinery that builds models no single rank can hold.
  • the pipe engine — layer-split parallelism driven by micro-batch schedules across a process topology.
  • the JIT op builder — a registry of fused kernels compiled on first use through ninja.

Why You Need This

The first reason is practical: the memory wall is the wall you hit. Train anything past a few billion parameters on commodity GPUs and PyTorch’s default data-parallel replicate-everything model stops fitting long before your compute does. ZeRO’s insight, implemented in three escalating stages, is that a training cluster wastes staggering amounts of memory by keeping identical optimizer states on every rank. Stage one partitions those states, stage two adds gradient partitioning, and stage three goes all the way and partitions the model parameters, gathering each layer on the fly only for the instants it is needed. When even stage three is not enough, the offload machinery spills states and parameters to CPU memory or NVMe storage, which is how a machine with modest GPUs can co-author a 176-billion-parameter run.

The second reason is the engineering itself. This codebase is a masterclass in the unglamorous systems work that papers skip: a prefetch coordinator that issues asynchronous parameter fetches before a layer needs them, a contiguous memory allocator that packs fragmented shards into bandwidth-friendly flat buffers, a tiling module that slices single enormous layers so they can pass through a sharded step, and a swap layer that moves optimizer state asynchronously so the GPU never stalls waiting for storage. None of these ideas is exotic in isolation, but seeing them composed inside one coherent engine is the difference between reading the ZeRO papers and understanding them.

The third reason is leverage. The abstractions pioneered here became the default vocabulary of the field: Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate, PyTorch Lightning, MosaicML Composer, Determined, and MMEngine all ship DeepSpeed integrations, and the research has kept moving with DeepSpeed-MoE, ZeRO++, Ulysses sequence parallelism, ZenFlow, SuperOffload, and DeepCompile arriving year after year. If you work with large models in any capacity, the patterns in this tree — partitioned parameters, hook-driven offload, schedule-driven collectives — reappear everywhere from inference servers to fine-tuning frameworks, and recognizing them by name makes every other system easier to read.

The detailed view: launcher and collectives at the top, the ZeRO internals block with its offload and prefetch machinery, the pipe-parallel subsystem, training support modules, and the platform layer underneath.

Start where every user starts: deepspeed/runtime/engine.py. The file runs to 5,153 lines, and the class DeepSpeedEngine opens at line 516 after a long module-level initialize() function has already read your config JSON and made the load-bearing decisions. From there the engine is a conventional training loop wearing a distributed coat: forward begins at line 2987, backward at 3386, the optimizer step at 3571, and checkpointing at save_checkpoint (line 4873) and load_checkpoint (line 4399), with train and eval entry points near lines 2887 and 2893. Along the way the engine wires in a timer module for the wallclock breakdowns you see in logs, and a small monitor dispatcher that routes metrics to TensorBoard, WandB, or CSV depending on your config. The elegance is that the user’s training script never changes shape — the engine intercepts the same three calls and adds bookkeeping between them.

The ZeRO block is where the memory actually gets saved. stage_1_and_2.py, at 3,464 lines, implements DeepSpeedZeroOptimizer: it flattens gradients, reduces and partitions them by rank, and hands the update to a fused optimizer — fused_optimizer.py, 456 lines, keeps FP16 master weights in a single flat buffer updated by one kernel call. Stage three is a different beast entirely. stage3.py, 3,435 lines, registers every parameter as a partition, and its companion partition_parameters.py, 2,093 lines, provides the zero.Init context so a model can be constructed from the start without any rank materializing the full weights. The runtime choreography lives in parameter_offload.py (552 lines), which pushes parameters to CPU or NVMe and swaps them back ahead of each forward and backward, and partitioned_param_coordinator.py (587 lines), which peeks at upcoming module executions to issue asynchronous prefetches so gathers overlap with compute. Supporting cast includes contiguous_memory_allocator.py for flat buffers, tiling.py (230 lines) for layers too big for one sharded pass, offload_states.py (87 lines) as a scoped context that lends the GPU to another workload, and a partitioned optimizer swapper in swap_tensor that moves states without blocking the step.

Parallelism beyond data-parallel lives in two places. The pipe subsystem mirrors a miniature framework: pipe/engine.py (1,153 lines) subclasses DeepSpeedEngine and buffers micro-batches, module.py (580 lines) lets you declare which layers live on which stage, schedule.py (486 lines) encodes the clock-cycle choreography of forwards, backwards, and buffer exchanges, topology.py (378 lines) models the process mesh where data, pipe, and model-parallel axes intersect, and p2p.py (136 lines) supplies the raw send and recv. Alongside it, sharded_moe.py (635 lines) implements DeepSpeed-MoE’s top-K expert routing with capacity-aware dispatch, and module_inject (replace_module.py at 632 lines plus a 26-line policy base) can swap standard transformer blocks for optimized kernels at load time. Combine data, pipe, and tensor axes and you get the 3D parallelism that carried the 530-billion-parameter runs.

Two subsystems make all of this operable. The launcher splits into launch.py (250 lines), the command-line front door, and runner.py (523 lines), which reads a hostfile into a resource pool, checks each host’s reachability over SSH, and honors a no-SSH mode for single-box runs — it is the piece that turns one command into a synchronized cluster. The autotuner (autotuner.py at 957 lines with a 352-line scheduler) runs training trials over a search space of ZeRO stages, offload targets, and micro-batch sizes, scores them with an exponential-median scheme, and writes the winning configuration back for production use. Underneath everything, the accelerator package defines a 326-line abstract device contract with concrete implementations for CUDA, CPU, Intel XPU, Ascend NPU, HPU for Gaudi, Apple MPS, and more, while comm.py (818 lines) wraps the collectives with timing hooks and a oneCCL backend so even CPU-only clusters can participate. The op builder registry, 839 lines, JIT-compiles the fused kernels on first use through ninja and torch’s extension machinery, caching results so the compile cost is paid once.

The research frontier is unusually visible in the tree. superoffload_stage3.py (320 lines) implements the SuperOffload engine for superchip hardware that earned an ASPLOS 2026 honorable mention; a zenflow package carries the stall-free offloading engine from its 2025 write-up; inference v2 has its own engine module. Recent news items trace the pace: Muon optimizer support and SDMA offloaded collectives for AMD GPUs landed in May 2026, a core API update in December 2025 added PyTorch-style backward hooks and low-precision master states, and ZeRO++ powered large-scale distillation for recommendation models at LinkedIn. Arctic Long Sequence Training pushed context windows into the millions of tokens, DeepNVMe made NVMe bandwidth a first-class citizen, and DeepCompile and AutoTP brought compiler-style and automatic tensor-parallel optimizations into the mix. The repository doubles as a living index of systems-for-ML research.

From Install to First Sharded Step

Installation is one pip command, and the ops compile on demand:

pip install deepspeed
ds_report
deepspeed --num_gpus=4 train.py --deepspeed_config ds_config.json

The ds_report command prints which compiled kernels are available and which will be built on first use, which is invaluable for debugging environments. Your training script changes by three lines: import deepspeed, wrap the model with deepspeed.initialize, and hand a JSON config that names the ZeRO stage and offload targets. A minimal stage-two config with CPU optimizer offload is a dozen lines of JSON. On Windows the project offers a build_win.bat script for pre-building, with a documented caveat that the asynchronous I/O and GDS offload backends are unsupported there. The launcher accepts a hostfile listing one hostname per line with slot counts, and from that moment your four-GPU workstation and your twelve-node cluster are driven by the same command.

Honest limits: DeepSpeed’s power is proportional to its config surface, and the many-knobbed JSON can feel like tuning a ship’s engine room for users who just want training to run; the JIT compilation path trades a slow first step for a fast install, which occasionally surfaces as environment-specific build errors; the pipe-parallel subsystem, while instructive, is the oldest architectural layer and shows its age next to newer schedule implementations elsewhere in the ecosystem; and the research features move quickly enough that a given release may carry experimental modules still settling down. None of that dims the core achievement: this is the codebase that made parameter sharding a solvable engineering problem rather than a research paper, and it repays every hour you spend inside it.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the DeepSpeed training engine: ZeRO stages one through three, the DeepSpeedEngine forward-backward-step loop, pipe parallelism, the multi-node launcher, and the accelerator layer that spans six hardware vendors.

entry.title: The Toolbox Behind Every Diffusion Model - Inside huggingface/diffusers

link.title: The Toolbox Behind Every Diffusion Model - Inside huggingface/diffusers

entry.content:
If you have generated an image with an open model in the last three years, the odds are high that the huggingface/diffusers library was somewhere underneath. It is the reference toolbox for diffusion models — image, video, and audio — and its design philosophy is printed in its own docs: usability over performance, simple over easy, customizability over abstractions. The repository under the Apache-2.0 license now contains ready-to-run flows for 85 model families, a scheduler library with dozens of sampling algorithms, and a runtime hook system that accelerates any model without touching its code.

The interesting engineering story is how the library keeps that sprawl coherent. Every model inherits one base class that handles saving, loading, and device placement. Every sampler obeys the same step contract, so you can trade DDIM for DPMSolver or flow matching without changing anything else in your script. Every end-to-end flow is ordinary Python you can read and fork. Around that core sits a loading layer for LoRA and adapters, a quantization layer for compressed checkpoints, and an accelerator layer of caching and offloading hooks. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview shows the four rings around the model core: samplers, end-to-end flows, loading and quantization, and the guidance and acceleration layer.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The model base class gives every architecture checkpoint saving, dtype handling, and device movement for free.
  • The attention processor file is the largest source file in the repo at over 4,500 lines, holding swappable attention implementations for every supported architecture.
  • The scheduler library implements sampling algorithms from classic DDIM to rectified flow, all behind one step interface.
  • The stable diffusion flow is the canonical read-first file: encode a prompt, denoise latents, decode pixels.
  • The modular composer assembles new flows from reusable blocks instead of copying a full flow.
  • The loader mixins graft LoRA weights onto models with cross-format key remapping.
  • The guidance module separates guidance strategies from both samplers and models.
  • The inference hooks stream layers between CPU and GPU so oversized models fit smaller cards.

Why You Need This

Reproducibility is the first reason. A generated image depends on the sampler, the guidance scale, the seed, and a dozen scheduling constants, and diffusers pins all of that in versioned, serializable configuration. The scheduler classes carry their beta schedules and timestep spacing as plain config objects, so a result published alongside its from_pretrained calls can be regenerated bit-for-bit. If you produce model comparisons, benchmark reports, or training artifacts, that discipline is the difference between a reproducible claim and a lucky screenshot.

The second reason is the modular swap-in architecture. Attention inside every model is delegated to processor classes, which means adding a new attention variant — or rerouting existing attention for control, editing, or IP-Adapter-style image conditioning via the adapter loader — happens without forking the model code. The same pattern extends to guidance strategies, where a dozen published guidance methods sit behind one interface, so experimenting with a research paper’s guidance becomes a one-line change rather than a rewrite of the denoising loop.

The third reason is the acceleration layer, which has quietly become one of the library’s most valuable parts. The hooks package implements step-skipping caches, the pyramid attention broadcast hook cuts redundant attention work on video models, and tensor parallel hooks split layers across GPUs. These attach to a loaded model with a couple of lines, which means you can benchmark three acceleration strategies on your own hardware and workload in an afternoon instead of rewriting model internals for each one.

The detail graph splits the library into six bands: model core, scheduler library, generation flows, loading, acceleration, and shared utilities.

Start in the model core at the top. The UNet2DConditionModel behind Stable Diffusion and the Transformer2DModel behind DiT-style models both compose from the same transformer block and embedding classes, and both route their attention through the processor layer with a runtime dispatcher choosing between native, flash, and memory-efficient kernels. That single routing decision explains how one codebase serves architectures from 2022 and 2026 without duplicating attention code.

The scheduler band rewards reading three files in order. DDIM shows the minimal step math, DPMSolver multistep shows how higher-order solvers reuse history to cut steps, and flow-match Euler shows the rectified-flow formulation that Flux and SD3 use. Shared beta-schedule machinery lives in scheduling_utils, and because every scheduler exposes the same contract, the flows above treat samplers as plug-ins.

The generation flows band is where the library meets users. The Stable Diffusion flow remains the best teaching artifact — its __call__ is one readable function from text encoding through latent denoising to image post-processing. The Flux flow shows the modern shape with guidance embeddings, SD3 demonstrates MMDiT wiring, and AnimateDiff shows video as a temporal extension of the same UNet features. On the loading side, single-file loading converts checkpoints saved by other tools into diffusers models, while training utilities support the official fine-tuning examples.

From Install to a First Image

Installation is a plain pip install diffusers alongside PyTorch and transformers. The shortest path to an image uses the library’s general loader class: import it from diffusers, call from_pretrained("stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5", torch_dtype=torch.float16), move the result to CUDA, and invoke it with a prompt — pipe("a photorealistic mountain lake at dawn").images[0]. From there the same object takes a different scheduler via pipe.scheduler = DDPMScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config), accepts LoRA weights through load_lora_weights, and gets faster through hook attachment. The examples directory mirrors this progression with fine-tuning scripts for control, inpainting, and video.

Honest limits: the library optimizes for usability over raw speed, so peak-throughput serving is better served by dedicated inference servers; diffusers is the toolbox you prototype and produce with, not a request-batching service. The 85-family breadth means API consistency varies at the edges — newer model flows sometimes ship with experimental interfaces that settle over releases. Memory requirements for video and large image models remain significant even with offloading, and quantized checkpoints trade some fidelity for accessibility. None of this dents the core achievement: a coherent, inspectable implementation of an entire research field that still runs in a few lines of Python.
entry.summary: How diffusers structures 85 model families around swappable denoising schedulers, attention processors, LoRA loading, and runtime acceleration hooks.

entry.title: The Config-Driven Engine Behind SDXL - Inside Stability-AI/generative-models

link.title: The Config-Driven Engine Behind SDXL - Inside Stability-AI/generative-models

entry.content:
Every image model has a lab notebook. For Stability AI’s flagship family, that notebook is generative-models, the repository where SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, Stable Video Diffusion, SV3D, and SV4D all live as research code. It is not a product and not a polished library — the README reads mostly as a dated changelog of model releases, from the November 2023 turbo announcement to the May 2025 arrival of Stable Video 4D 2.0. What holds the whole thing together is one idea: almost nothing about a model is written in Python. Architectures, losses, schedulers, even the number of camera views in a 4D rollout are declared in YAML files under configs/ and assembled at startup, so the same codebase can describe a toy MNIST experiment and a 576x576 four-dimensional video generator with the same grammar.

The assembly mechanism is a function called instantiate_from_config, defined in sgm/util.py. Every config entry carries a target — a fully qualified class path such as sgm.models.diffusion.DiffusionEngine — plus a params dictionary, and the loader imports the class and hands it the params, recursively, all the way down. That single convention is the spine of the repository: main.py is a thin PyTorch Lightning shell, the sgm/ package is a shelf of interchangeable parts, and a YAML file is the decision about which parts click together. Reading this codebase therefore feels less like reading a program and more like reading a catalog of parts plus a stack of assembly instructions. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

From the training entry point and its YAML wiring, through the conditioner and the diffusion engine, down to the denoiser framework and the demo scripts that drive everything.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The training entry point parses config files, merges them left to right, and hands the result to PyTorch Lightning — 868 lines that mostly stay out of the way.
  • The example training config declares a full text-to-image model as nested target-and-params blocks, dataloader, loss, and all.
  • The instantiation helper turns those target strings into live objects and wires together the graph the config describes.
  • The DiffusionEngine is the training-and-sampling chassis, formerly known as LatentDiffusion, holding the network, conditioner, first-stage autoencoder, and loss in one class.
  • The conditioner hosts GeneralConditioner, one 921-line class that aggregates text, image, crop, and aesthetic embeddings behind a single batch interface.
  • The video model extends the image UNet with temporal attention layers — 1,170 lines that turn stills into motion.
  • The denoiser wraps the network in sigma space so noise levels, input scaling, and loss weighting are swappable parts rather than hardcoded habits.
  • The samplers implement Euler, Heun, and DPM++ 2M solvers, while guiders handle classifier-free guidance as a fully independent axis.

Why You Need This

First, the config system is dependency injection with no framework attached. When main.py loads a file, it parses every block, follows each target string to a Python class, and calls the class with the block’s params — so a “model” in this repository is literally a tree of importable class paths. Because every part is addressable, a research experiment becomes a diff in YAML instead of a fork in Python: swap the conditioner, change the first-stage autoencoder, retarget the loss, and the training script never changes. Configs merge left to right, so a shared base file plus a small override file is the idiomatic way to describe an ablation. The toy MNIST config bundled under configs/example_training shows the same machinery scaled down to a dataset you can actually run overnight, which makes it the best first file to read. This is also how one repository ships image models, video models, and 4D models without becoming three separate codebases — the difference between them is data, mostly.

Second, the denoiser framework is the clearest modern view of how diffusion models are actually organized. Older codebases hardcode one training objective deep inside a model class; this repository refuses to. A diffusion step is decomposed into a network, a sigma schedule drawn by sigma_sampling, input scaling handled by a scaling module, loss weighting handled by a weighting module, and the discretization that maps timesteps to sigmas lives in discretizer.py. The denoiser.py file itself is only 61 lines — it composes those parts, and the scaling and weighting modules it delegates to stay under fifty lines each, proof of how much mileage a clean interface buys. When SDXL-Turbo arrived with adversarial diffusion distillation and needed radically different noise handling, it slotted in as different scaling and weighting choices rather than a rewrite, and the EDM-style samplers in sampling.py consume the same sigma interface.

Third, conditioning is unified in a way worth copying. GeneralConditioner in encoders/modules.py is one class that owns every conditioner variant — frozen text encoders, image embedders, the original-size, crop-coordinates, and aesthetic-score vectors that SDXL famously conditions on — and flattens them into a batch dict the network can consume. Each sub-conditioner registers the keys it can provide, the output carries only what the target network asks for, and the numeric vectors ride beside the text embeddings — the concrete mechanics behind SDXL’s size, crop, and aesthetic conditioning. Reading that one file teaches you what SDXL’s “additional conditioning” actually is, because every vector it emits is named, counted, and concatenated in plain sight. Add the autoencoder package, whose regularizers include the vector-quantization codebook logic in quantize.py, and you have the complete anatomy of a latent diffusion system in one readable shelf.

The detail view: demo entry scripts, the enum-driven Python sampling facade, the denoiser's four-part decomposition, and the module zoo underneath.

The detail diagram starts at the demo layer, which is how most people meet this repository. scripts/demo/sampling.py is a 308-line Streamlit application that loads a model from checkpoints/, builds a value dictionary with prompt, negative prompt, and sizing vectors, and calls do_sample; video_sampling.py extends the same pattern to 257 lines for SVD and SV3D. turbo.py, at 186 lines, is the distilled-model demo, and the community-built gradio_app.py plus gradio_app_sv4d.py wrap the video models in a friendlier UI. There is also a forensics tool: detect.py uses the invisible-watermark library to extract the watermark embedded in generated images, which is a rare example of provenance tooling shipping next to the model code.

The most underrated file is sgm/inference/api.py, a 327-line programmatic surface that compresses the entire YAML zoo into four enums: ModelArchitecture, Sampler, Discretization, and Guider. Its SamplingParams dataclass fixes the production defaults — 1024 by 1024 output, 50 steps, the DPM++ 2M solver, guidance scale 6.0, and the EDM sigma range from 0.0292 to 14.6146 — and its spec table maps SDXL base and refiner checkpoints, both 0.9 and 1.0, to their configs. From there you get text_to_image, image_to_image with a strength parameter, and a refiner method that skips encoding and applies the well-known aesthetic scores of 6.0 against 2.5. If you want to see how a research codebase grows a usable face without abandoning its config roots, this is the file to study.

Beneath the demos sits the module zoo. openaimodel.py, at 823 lines, is the UNet that every diagram starts with, while model.py in the same folder holds the encoder and decoder bodies at 657 lines; the autoencoder package adds latent-space regularizers on top, including the quantize.py codebook machinery. The video scripts show how the family scales in time: simple_video_sample.py runs SVD and SV3D, simple_video_sample_4d.py adds reference multi-views at 238 lines, and simple_video_sample_4d2.py, at 220 lines, generates 48 frames as 12 video frames times 4 camera views, then rolls autoregressively in 12-frame windows to reach longer clips. Same latent interface, one extra axis at a time.

The release timeline inside the README doubles as a history of latent video generation. In November 2023 the repository shipped SDXL-Turbo with adversarial diffusion distillation and, a week later, Stable Video Diffusion with 14- and 25-frame variants at 576 by 1024. March 2024 brought SV3D, an orbital-camera model generating 21 frames from a single object image, in an unconstrained orbital version and a path-controlled one. July 2024 added SV4D, which consumes five context frames plus eight SV3D reference views to emit 40 frames, and the May 2025 SV4D 2.0 improved fidelity, generalized to real-world footage without needing those reference views, and rolls autoregressively in 12-frame windows for longer outputs. Every one of those steps reused the same engine files, which is the whole point.

From Install to First Image

The repository is a Hatch-packaged Python project with no pinned dependencies, and the README prescribes a CUDA 11.8 environment. Getting a first image is a weights problem more than a code problem: download an SDXL checkpoint into checkpoints/, then launch the Streamlit demo.

git clone https://github.com/Stability-AI/generative-models.git
cd generative-models
python3.10 -m venv .generativemodels
source .generativemodels/bin/activate
pip3 install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118
pip3 install -r requirements/pt2.txt
pip3 install .
# place a model checkpoint in checkpoints/
streamlit run scripts/demo/sampling.py

For the video-to-4D flagship, the README’s quickstart is a single line once sv4d2.safetensors is in checkpoints/: run scripts/sampling/simple_video_sample_4d2.py with an input gif or mp4 and an output folder. Flags like encoding_t and decoding_t control how many frames are encoded or decoded at once for low-VRAM GPUs, and img_size drops the working resolution to 512.

Honest limits: this is research code, not an SDK. Dependencies are deliberately unpinned, the README is a news column rather than documentation, and several model releases live in their own branches or configs that assume you read the release notes first. The code is MIT licensed in LICENSE-CODE, but the weights are not in the repository and carry separate terms — CreativeML Open RAIL++-M for SDXL 1.0 and research-only licenses for the 0.9 and video models. Training at scale assumes the separate sdata data-loading repository and webdataset-formatted corpora, and comfortable VRAM budgets. None of that diminishes the code: for a config-driven architecture pattern and a still-current definition of what a diffusion model is made of, generative-models remains the reference shelf.
entry.summary: How Stability AI's generative-models repository wires SDXL, video diffusion, and 4D synthesis from YAML: an instantiate_from_config kernel, a sigma-space denoiser framework, and one conditioner for every prompt.

entry.title: The Training Rig Behind Pythia - Inside EleutherAI/gpt-neox

link.title: The Training Rig Behind Pythia - Inside EleutherAI/gpt-neox

entry.content:
Some of the most influential language models of the open-source era were trained by a volunteer collective with no vendor behind them. GPT-NeoX is EleutherAI’s library for training large-scale autoregressive language models on GPU clusters, built on NVIDIA’s Megatron design and DeepSpeed’s ZeRO machinery, and released under the Apache 2.0 license. Its track record is extraordinary for a research codebase: GPT-NeoX-20B, one of the first capable open weights of its size, the entire Pythia scaling suite from 70 million to 12 billion parameters, StableLM for Stability AI, RedPajama-INCITE for Together, and FORGE at Oak Ridge National Laboratory all came out of this tree. The project counts more than 40 organizations, more than 50 models, and more than 60 publications in its USERS.md ledger, and it has run at scale on Frontier, Summit, LUMI, Leonardo, AWS, and CoreWeave on both NVIDIA and AMD hardware.

The repository rewards reading precisely because it refuses to hide the machinery. One YAML file names your architecture, another names your cluster, and the code meets you at the intersection: a launcher that merges configs and spawns processes, a typed argument object that every subsystem reads, Megatron-style sharded layers, a pipe-parallel wrapper, a memory-mapped data path, and checkpoint tooling that uploads straight to blob storage. It is a complete answer to the question of how billion-parameter training is actually organized. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

GPT-NeoX overview: deepy merges configs and launches training, NeoXArgs drives the pretrain loop, which builds sharded transformer models, feeds them mmap-backed data, and checkpoints into storage with JIT-compiled kernels alongside.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • the deepy launcher wrapper — merges your YAML files and hands them to the DeepSpeed launcher, one process per GPU.
  • the train entry point — a few dozen lines that consume arguments and call pretrain.
  • the NeoXArgs configuration system — every knob of the framework merged into one validated object.
  • the training loop — pretrain, forward_step, train_step, and evaluate in a 1,679-line module.
  • the sharded transformer — attention and feedforward blocks cut across tensor-parallel ranks.
  • the parallel layers — column and row parallel linears with vocab-parallel embeddings.
  • the data loaders — blended, sampled iterators over memory-mapped token files.
  • the JIT fused kernels — softmax and rotary kernels compiled on demand for NVIDIA and AMD.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that this is the most readable large-scale trainer in the open-source ecosystem. Where production frameworks interleave abstraction layers until the actual training step is unfindable, GPT-NeoX keeps an almost textbook layout: configuration in one directory, model in another, model-parallel utilities in a third, and a single training module that ties them together. If you have ever wanted to see, in one file, how gradient accumulation, ZeRO steps, gradient noise scale tracking, and evaluation interleave across a real 20-billion-parameter run, the answer is a 1,679-line Python module you can read in an afternoon.

The second reason is architectural literacy. The Megatron patterns implemented here — column-parallel and row-parallel linears, vocab-parallel embeddings that shard the token table, activations gathered and scattered between ranks — became the de facto vocabulary of every serious training stack. The repository also demonstrates the operational side that papers never show: hostfiles and pdsh, MPI and Slurm launchers, no-SSH modes for clusters that forbid direct connections, Docker and Apptainer deployments for national-lab systems, WandB and Comet monitoring, Nsight profiling hooks, and a checkpoint uploader. These are the unglamorous skills that decide whether a training run finishes at all.

The third reason is the model zoo hiding in the model directory. Beyond the standard attention stack you will find a dropless mixture-of-experts implementation routed with Sinkhorn balancing, a Mamba state-space block, RWKV v6 layers with their own CUDA kernel, gMLP blocks, rotary and AliBi positional schemes, and a Transformer Engine swap-in for Hopper-class GPUs. Each is written against the same sharded-layer interface, which makes the directory one of the best comparative anatomy lessons in modern architecture design available anywhere.

The detailed view: entry points on the left, the configuration merge in the middle, the training loop with its diagnostics, the model zoo, model-parallel utilities, and the data and kernel layer at the bottom.

The flow starts with deepy.py, the only command most users ever run. It calls NeoXArgs.consume_deepy_args to merge an arbitrary number of YAML files — later files override earlier ones, which is how the project composes a model config with a cluster config — injects a WandB API key into worker environments if one is configured, and then calls DeepSpeed’s launcher to replicate the script across every GPU in the hostfile. train.py is deliberately tiny: consume the merged arguments, configure distributed settings, build the tokenizer, initialize TensorBoard or Comet if requested, and call pretrain. eval.py and generate.py reuse the same argument system, so evaluation through the lm-evaluation-harness and text sampling both ride the identical configuration path into the loop. The heart of the argument system is the neox_arguments package: arguments.py (1,353 lines) handles merging and validation, neox_args.py (1,325 lines) declares every field as dataclass entries with documentation, and deepspeed_args.py (264 lines) translates user intent into the zero_optimization dictionaries DeepSpeed expects.

pretrain() in megatron/training.py is where the run takes shape. It calls initialize_megatron (194 lines) for process groups and seeds, builds the model through get_model (line 901), which returns a GPT2ModelPipe when pipe-parallel sizes are nonzero — that class, in gpt2_model.py, subclasses the pipe-module base and assigns layers to stages — then builds the optimizer (line 990) and learning-rate scheduler (line 1139), and enters the train loop at line 1465. Each iteration passes through train_step (line 1318) or its pipe variant train_step_pipe (line 1423), with backward_step at line 1299 and forward_step at line 564 handling the gradients and loss. Woven through it are timers, logging (a 537-line module feeding WandB, Comet, and TensorBoard), gradient noise scale tracking (181 lines), and muP parameter scaling support (196 lines). Evaluation lives at line 1618, and checkpointing flows through megatron/checkpointing.py (423 lines): save_ds_checkpoint at line 181, argument re-validation at line 53, old-tag pruning at line 158, and an upload_checkpoint path at line 315 that pushes artifacts to blob storage so a cluster job never dies with its weights locked inside.

The model block is the conceptual center. transformer.py (1,084 lines) defines ParallelMLP at line 88, ParallelSelfAttention at line 268, and ParallelTransformerLayer at line 908, plus pipe-aware subclasses at the bottom of the file. Everything heavy inside those blocks delegates to mpu/layers.py (720 lines): VocabParallelEmbedding at line 98 shards the vocabulary table across ranks so no GPU holds all embedding rows, ColumnParallelLinear at line 383 and RowParallelLinear at line 589 cut weight matrices along input or output dimensions, and the weight-initialization helpers at the top handle the delicate case of initializing sharded matrices identically on every rank. mpu/mappings.py (364 lines) supplies the gather/scatter glue and mpu/initialize.py (289 lines) builds the process groups these layers query at construction time.

Around that core, the zoo rotates through alternatives: moe_mlp.py (370 lines) and router.py (232 lines) implement dropless experts on the tensor-parallel group with Sinkhorn routing; transformer_engine.py (594 lines) swaps the block internals for NVIDIA’s TE kernels on Ampere and Hopper; positional_embeddings.py (217 lines) offers rotary and AliBi as interchangeable attention biases; and the fused_kernels package JIT-compiles masked-softmax and rotary kernels from .h and .cu sources, adapting to AMD’s MI100 and MI250X toolchains without code changes. The data side mirrors this discipline: preprocessing writes a .bin and .idx pair whose format is implemented twice, once in indexed_dataset.py (483 lines) as a mmap reader and once in helpers.cpp (671 lines) as the C++ extension that wrote it, and gpt2_dataset.py (447 lines) slices those token streams into fixed-length training sequences. A pairwise dataset module for preference-style records and a small sampler family round out the directory, so post-training data flows through the same loaders as pretraining. When training is done, tools/ckpts/convert_neox_to_hf.py exports checkpoints to GPTNeoX, Llama, or Mistral architectures for inference, and the post-training directory carries DPO, KTO, REINFORCE, reward-model, and SFT recipes with Llama 3 configs included.

From Install to a 125-Million-Parameter Run

The README’s supported range is Python 3.8 through 3.10 and PyTorch 1.8 through 2.0, and the whole journey fits in three commands:

pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt
python prepare_data.py -d ./data
python ./deepy.py train.py -d configs 125M.yml local_setup.yml

prepare_data.py downloads and tokenizes a sample dataset into the .bin and .idx pair the loaders expect. The -d flag sets a config directory prefix, so the model definition in 125M.yml combines with your local hardware settings in local_setup.yml — the README explicitly recommends this split of model parameters from data-path parameters. One notable dependency warning: the code relies on DeeperSpeed, EleutherAI’s fork of DeepSpeed, and the project strongly recommends a virtual environment because the fork can conflict with stock DeepSpeed installs elsewhere on the machine. Fused kernels compile on first launch, or you can pre-build them from a Python shell. For multi-node work, a hostfile with one “hostname slots=8” line per machine is all the launcher needs, whether you arrive via pdsh, MPI, or Slurm.

Honest limits: this is a pretraining rig, not a serving stack, and the README itself redirects inference users to Hugging Face Transformers; the dependency set is heavy and version-sensitive, anchored to a DeepSpeed fork that wants environment isolation; the configuration surface, while superbly documented, runs to hundreds of fields that interact in ways only experience teaches; and the smallest interesting runs still want a multi-GPU machine, so the barrier to a first experiment is a real GPU, not a laptop. None of that changes the essentials: this is the codebase that democratized billion-parameter pretraining, and its blend of readable structure and hard-won scale lessons makes it one of the most valuable trees an ML engineer can walk through.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the GPT-NeoX training library: the deepy launcher, NeoXArgs configuration merging, Megatron-style sharded layers, pipe-parallel model wiring, the mmap data flow, and the model zoo from Mamba to RWKV.

entry.title: Node Graphs for Professional Image Work - Inside invoke-ai/InvokeAI

link.title: Node Graphs for Professional Image Work - Inside invoke-ai/InvokeAI

entry.content:
While most Stable Diffusion interfaces grew from scripts into apps, InvokeAI took the opposite path: it was designed from the start as a professional creative tool, and the codebase shows it. The current repository is a full-stack application — a TypeScript React canvas and workflow editor on the front, a FastAPI service layer in the middle, and a typed node-graph execution engine underneath that turns every generation into a composable graph of invocations. It ships under the InvokeAI license, an Apache-2.0 derivative that permits commercial use, and the README states plainly that it serves as the foundation for commercial products.

What makes the source worth a tour is the graph engine at its center. Every operation in the app — loading a Flux model, denoising latents, applying a ControlNet, upscaling — is an invocation: a strongly typed node with declared inputs and outputs. Queued sessions persist in a database, batches expand across seeds and prompts, and a session processor walks each graph and emits progress over sockets to the React client. Around that spine sits a model manager with VRAM-aware caching, quantization support down to NVFP4, and invocation families for an unusually wide range of architectures, including video. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview traces the path from a click in the React canvas, through the queue and processor, into the invocation library and the model backend.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The React web app hosts the unified canvas and the node-graph workflow editor in one TypeScript workspace.
  • The FastAPI application mounts REST routers and a Socket.IO bridge that streams progress events to the browser.
  • The REST routers cover sessions, models, boards, style presets, and videos in roughly twenty files.
  • The session queue persists every queued graph with its batch expansions and execution history.
  • The session processor pulls the next session and executes node by node as inputs become ready.
  • The base invocation class gives every node a generated schema, type ID, and invoke contract.
  • The denoise latents node is the architectural crossroads where conditioning meets any supported model.
  • The model manager records, installs, and loads models through a VRAM-aware cache with quantization support.

Why You Need This

The graph engine is the first reason. Tools that hardcode a generation flow hit a wall the moment a professional workflow needs something custom — two models in sequence, a mask pulled from a segmentation node, an upscale between denoise passes. InvokeAI solves this structurally: every capability is an invocation with typed fields, and the session processor executes arbitrary graphs of them with persistence and resume. The batch module then expands one graph across seeds, prompts, and models — linearizing a whole design exploration into a queue you can walk away from.

The second reason is the model layer. The model manager treats models as first-class records with metadata, install flows, and starter sets, and the load path routes each model type to the right loader through a VRAM-aware cache that keeps hot models resident and evicts the rest. For large architectures, the quantization package offers FP8, NVFP4, and bitsandbytes schemes with explicit load plans, which is how multi-billion-parameter image and video models fit on single consumer cards at all.

The third reason is architecture breadth executed through one interface. The invocation library contains complete node families for Flux, SD3, and the Wan video models, plus ControlNet and upscaling nodes that work across families. Reading how a new architecture is added — backend code under invokeai/backend, a denoiser invocation, loader nodes — is a practical education in supporting many diffusion models without forking the application each time.

The detail graph separates six bands: React frontend, API layer, graph engine, invocation library, model backend, and platform services.

Start at the frontend band. The app organizes state into feature modules per domain — generation, canvas, nodes, gallery — and the workbench composes them into the unified canvas where layers, masks, and prompts coexist. Every action talks to the backend through the FastAPI app, whose routers receive services by dependency injection and whose socket bridge pushes queue and progress events so the UI stays live during long generations.

The graph engine band shows the execution contract. A submitted graph lands in the session queue as a persisted row with its batch expansion, the session processor walks nodes whose inputs are satisfied, and field plumbing carries typed values between node outputs and inputs. Primitive nodes seed graphs with images, latents, and integers, which is how a simple text-to-image request becomes just another graph.

The model and services bands complete the picture. The model manager hands each model to the right loader, quantization applies through load plans, and architecture backends like Flux implement the actual denoising math with runtime patching for LoRAs. On the platform side, gallery, image storage, events, and a resumable download service give the app its product feel — results land in boards, model downloads survive interruptions, and everything streams through one event bus.

From Install to a First Image

The supported path is the standalone Launcher, downloadable from the project’s releases page, which installs and updates Invoke in its own environment; the docs also cover manual installation for custom setups. Start the server with invokeai-web --root ~/invokeai and open the printed local URL. New users should start in the canvas: pick a model in the manager, enter a prompt, and generate — every result lands in a board with its full settings attached for recall. The workflow editor sits one tab away: build a graph by adding nodes, link their typed fields, queue it, and watch each node light up as the processor reaches it. The invocation API also lets external tools submit graphs over HTTP.

Honest limits: this is a heavier application than a simple web UI — the frontend build, database, and service layer demand more RAM and setup patience than minimal tools, and the node graph, while powerful, has a learning curve that casual users may not want. Hardware expectations are professional: large Flux or video models really want a 16 GB or better GPU even with quantization, and older cards are left behind by some new architectures. Because the project moves fast, workflows saved from older versions occasionally need revalidation after upgrades. For creative professionals who need reproducible, composable workflows rather than one-shot images, though, the investment pays for itself quickly.
entry.summary: How InvokeAI pairs a React canvas with a typed node-graph execution engine, a VRAM-aware model cache, and per-architecture invocation families from Flux to Wan video.

entry.title: The Executable That Is Also a Zip of Weights - Inside Mozilla-Ocho/llamafile

link.title: The Executable That Is Also a Zip of Weights - Inside Mozilla-Ocho/llamafile

entry.content:
Software distribution is the quiet bottleneck of local AI. Weights live in one place, runtimes in another, and every OS wants a different installer. The llamafile answer is almost absurd in its simplicity: take llama.cpp, compile it with Cosmopolitan Libc into an Actually Portable Executable that boots on six operating systems without installation, then append the model weights to the binary as a zip archive. The result is one file you can copy to a USB stick, double-click on Windows, chmod and run on Linux or macOS, and it opens a chat server on localhost. Announced by Mozilla Builders in November 2023 and revamped by Mozilla.ai since, the project has grown into a family — whisperfile for speech-to-text, diffusionfile for image generation, and a new agentfile that ships a configured agent as a single file.

The source tree is a masterclass in doing a lot with a little. The heart of the trick lives in a few thousand lines of C: llamafile.c opens the running executable as a zip store, reads the central directory from its last 64 kilobytes, and memory-maps the weights that sit after the program bytes. Around that core sit hand-written CPU matrix kernels with per-CPU-generation dispatch, runtime-loadable GPU backends for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and Vulkan, a complete line editor, and a chatbot family that shares one serving core across TUI, CLI, and HTTP modes. Almost none of it is Python, and almost none of it needs to be. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

From the launcher through the zip-of-weights packaging core and the chat family, over to the compute backends and the single-file siblings that reuse the same trick.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The launcher parses top-level arguments and routes the chat, CLI, and server modalities.
  • The packaging core opens the running executable as a zip store and validates the claimed size against the real one before mapping weights.
  • The zip reader scans the central directory in the file’s last 64KB to find what was appended.
  • The chatbot core holds the model, context, sampler, and an mtmd multimodal context shared by every mode.
  • The terminal UI is the interactive chat, built on a 160KB vendored line editor with highlighting.
  • The HTTP server exposes the same conversation to other programs on the network.
  • The backend loader discovers runtime GPU libraries, while TinyBLAS CPU kernels carry machines with no GPU at all.
  • The agentfile runner extends the one-file promise from models to agents — model, system prompt, and tool allowlist in a single executable.

Why You Need This

First, the packaging idea deserves study on its own merits, whatever your interest in AI. An APE binary from Cosmopolitan Libc is a real executable on multiple operating systems at once, and llamafile exploits the format’s tolerance for trailing data: model weights are appended exactly the way a zip appends files, so the same bytes are a program on Linux and weights on disk. llamafile.c reads the final 64KB for the central-directory magic, cross-checks the directory’s claimed size against the file on disk, and maps content with reference counting so multiple consumers can share one mapping. There is no installation step because there is nothing to install — the loader, the inference engine, and the model travel together. Portability starts at compile time, too: the cosmocc toolchain ships its own make, ar, and zipobj utilities, and build/config.mk pins the version it expects. One honest constraint comes with the trick: Windows refuses to execute images larger than 4GB, which is why bigger models ship as a separate GGUF next to the binary.

Second, the compute layer is a museum of performance engineering you can actually read. TinyBLAS is the project’s dependency-free answer to BLAS libraries: tinyblas_cpu.h dispatches matrix multiplication across AVX, AVX2, AVX512F, AVX-VNNI, FMA, Zen 4, and ARM v8.2 paths, iqk_mul_mat.inc carries the quantized-weight kernels in a 133KB include, and tinyblas.cu reimplements the same primitives in CUDA so NVIDIA GPUs work without a proprietary dependency in the binary. GPU backends are shared libraries loaded at runtime — built by cuda.sh, rocm.sh, or vulkan.sh, with Metal compiled on demand on Apple silicon using only the Xcode Command Line Tools. The design keeps the base binary small and lets a user add acceleration without rebuilding anything.

Third, the chatbot family shows how to share one core across interfaces without a framework. chatbot_main.cpp declares the global state — model, context, sampler, chat templates, and an mtmd context for multimodal inputs — and every mode plugs into it: the REPL for humans who like terminals, the CLI for one-shot questions with an –image flag, the HTTP API for programs. Input handling is split into small files, with chatbot_eval.cpp pulling images out of base64 data URIs through datauri.cpp before the model sees them. A describe_compute helper answers the first question every user has — where inference is actually running today — and the rework gave the TUI direct access to modern multimodal models through the mtmd API, with think-mode toggles intact. The 0.10 rework, documented candidly in README_0.10.0.md, rebuilt all of this on a current llama.cpp so recent models like Qwen3.5 work, trading away some of the classic experience — and the project kept the old releases available for anyone who preferred them.

The detail view: packaging and input handling, the chat family's five modes, the compute backend tree, the benchmarking tool, and agentfile's callback-ordered design.

The family branch is where the single-file idea compounds. whisperfile wraps whisper.cpp for transcription and translation, complete with a streaming server, microphone capture helpers like mic2txt and slurp, and even man pages. transcribefile is a leaner transcription command from the same module. diffusionfile bundles stable-diffusion.cpp so text-to-image joins the party. localscore is a benchmarking tool that reports tokens per second while a power sampler draws watts from NVML on NVIDIA cards and RSMI on AMD — measurement infrastructure most projects never ship. The README badges pin the foundations — llama.cpp at one commit, whisper.cpp at another — so a downloaded file tells you exactly which engine generation it carries, a discipline running from the 0.9-era LLaVA v1.5 files through today’s Qwen3.5 bundle. Each of these is the same recipe: a Cosmopolitan build, weights or assets in the zip, one focused purpose, and voice or image input that starts working the moment the file is executable.

The newest sibling, agentfile, is the most interesting because its DESIGN.md is a design course in sixteen kilobytes. The promise: preconfigure an agent — model, system prompt, tool allowlist — and share it as one file that runs anywhere, one-shot by default. Tools come from llama.cpp’s server-tools registry through a single adapter, with native get-datetime, HTTPS fetch over mbedtls, and web search built in so the file never depends on the host’s curl.
