The callback ordering is documented with reasons: the session recorder registers before confirmation, and the tracer after the iteration cap, so spans measure execution rather than the time a human spent deciding. Even failure handling is specified — when tool-call parsing fails, a heuristic scan lifts tool-call blocks out of the reply so a stubborn model does not kill the loop. Tool settings and record files are validated before GPU init and model load, so a bad flag fails in milliseconds instead of after a long checkpoint read. Context discipline is engineered too: replies re-render byte-stable with reasoning split into its own channel, so the KV prefix survives turns — on hybrid models a rewind would otherwise force a full re-prefill — and a tool-call grammar can stay dormant inside thinking tags.

The build system itself is worth a look. The Makefile wires together vendored modules — llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, stable-diffusion.cpp, and agent.cpp as pinned submodules with local patch sets — into Cosmopolitan’s o// output tree, using the cosmocc toolchain that a make setup target provisions. GPU targets like make cuda or make rocm build the runtime-loadable backends separately. It is old-school modular C at a scale few projects attempt anymore, and the repository layout mirrors it exactly, one clean directory per module.

From Download to First Chat

For most people the build is optional — the prebuilt files are the product. One download runs everywhere; Windows users add an .exe extension.

curl -LO https://huggingface.co/mozilla-ai/llamafile_0.10/resolve/main/Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.llamafile
chmod +x Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.llamafile
./Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.llamafile

The 0.8B Qwen3.5 file is the smallest official example and opens a browser chat on localhost. Building from source is a make setup for the toolchain, then make — with the GPU backend targets optional extras. The llamafile binary also runs external GGUF weights, which is the recommended path for anything over the 4GB Windows ceiling.

Honest limits: this is systems software with sharp edges. The Cosmopolitan toolchain is unusual and can fight mainstream CI and IDE assumptions; GPU support varies by platform, with some backends needing on-demand compilation; the 0.10 rework explicitly dropped features people liked, and the README says so rather than pretending otherwise. Bundling weights into executables also means redistribution inherits the model’s license, not just Apache 2.0 on the code — the llama.cpp and whisper.cpp changes are MIT specifically to stay upstreamable. And single-file convenience stops at 4GB on Windows, no way around it. The main documentation also lives at docs.mozilla.ai rather than in the tree, and the classic 0.9 behavior remains a separate download. But as a demonstration that local AI can be as easy to run as a text editor, and as a source to study for portable C, zip tricks, and kernel-level performance tuning, llamafile is in a class of its own.
entry.summary: How llamafile fuses llama.cpp with Cosmopolitan Libc into one double-clickable file: a zip central directory hiding inside an ELF header, TinyBLAS CPU kernels, and a whole family of whisperfile, diffusionfile, and agentfile siblings.

entry.title: One Token That Unlocks the Image - Inside haotian-liu/LLaVA

link.title: One Token That Unlocks the Image - Inside haotian-liu/LLaVA

entry.content:
Every multimodal assistant that chats about images owes something to this repository. LLaVA — Large Language and Vision Assistant — is the research codebase behind visual instruction tuning, the NeurIPS 2023 oral that showed a frozen CLIP encoder, a frozen Vicuna language model, and one tiny trainable bridge between them could follow complex instructions about pictures. Its successor LLaVA-1.5 then reached state of the art on eleven benchmarks using only public data, training in about a day on a single eight-A100 node. The insight was deceptively simple: you do not need to co-train vision and language from scratch, you need to teach an LLM to read a grid of image features as if they were tokens.

The repository stays as small as the idea. Strip away evaluation scripts and demo servers, and the entire model is a few hundred lines: a constants file whose most important number is IMAGE_TOKEN_INDEX = -200, a mixin that splices projected image features into a token stream, a regex-parsed two-layer MLP, and a frozen CLIP tower. Everything else — the training recipe, the worker cluster, the chat templates — is scaffolding around that splice. It is one of the few famous papers whose full method you can verify by reading the source in an afternoon. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

From the chat entry points through the controller-and-worker serving cluster, the checkpoint loader, and the vision-language bridge, over to the two-stage training script.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The CLI chats about an image from the terminal, with 4-bit quantization keeping the 7B model under 8GB of VRAM.
  • The Gradio web server renders the browser chat and polls the controller for newly launched models.
  • The controller keeps a registry of GPU workers with heartbeats and dispatches by lottery or shortest queue.
  • The model worker boots one checkpoint and streams generations, registering itself every fifteen seconds.
  • The builder is load_pretrained_model, resolving merged, projector-only, unmerged-LoRA, and bitsandbytes-quantized layouts.
  • The architecture mixin splits the token sequence at the image placeholder and interleaves image embeddings between the text gaps.
  • The CLIP tower runs frozen at 336 pixels and hands over patch features from the second-to-last layer.
  • The training script implements the two-stage recipe — 558K caption-alignment pairs, then the 665K-mixture visual instruction tuning set.

Why You Need This

First, this is the clearest existing lesson in what a multimodal LLM actually is. The answer, at the source level, is: a normal LLM whose input embedding matrix occasionally receives image features instead of token embeddings. In llava_arch.py, prepare_inputs_labels_for_multimodal finds every position where input_ids equals -200, embeds the surrounding text chunks as usual, and concatenates the projected image features into the gap — then rebuilds labels with IGNORE_INDEX over the image positions so the loss only trains on text. No new attention type, no fusion layer, no cross-attention. A 576-patch image becomes 576 soft tokens. Once you have read that function, the entire genre of vision-language models loses its mystique, because most of them are variations on this splice.

Second, the training recipe is a masterclass in doing less. Stage one connects the frozen tower to the frozen LLM by training only the projector on 558K caption pairs — the code enforces this with requires_grad flags, and the checkpoint that matters is a single mm_projector.bin. Stage two unfreezes the LLM and tunes on the 665K mixture with hyperparameters borrowed from Vicuna: global batch 256 at learning rate 1e-3 for pretrain, 128 at 2e-5 for finetune, one epoch each. The published wall-clock numbers make the point better than adjectives: pretraining takes 3.5 hours for the 7B on eight A100s, and instruction tuning about ten hours at 40GB or twenty at 80GB. The trainer adds two quietly clever touches — a modality-length-grouped sampler that batches image samples and text samples separately for a reported 25 percent speedup, and a separate learning rate for projector parameters. The paper’s efficiency was not hardware luck; it is visible as flags.

Third, the serving cluster is a miniature of production architecture. Controller, web server, and workers are separate processes talking over HTTP, with heartbeats every fifteen seconds and a thirty-second expiration that removes dead workers. Dispatch is a two-entry enum — lottery or shortest queue — and each worker reports its speed and queue length in a plain dataclass, so a new checkpoint becomes visible in the UI the moment it registers. The SGLang worker even shows how to route the same LLaVA conversation format to a high-throughput third-party backend. For anyone who has wondered how multi-model demo deployments keep a live model list, this is the smallest complete example we know of.

The detail view: the serving cluster's five processes, the bridge with its three LLM backends, the vision stack, the training machinery, and the evaluation harness.

The detail diagram’s bridge group shows the mixin pattern that keeps the model portable. LlavaMetaModel and LlavaMetaForCausalLM live once in llava_arch.py, and the three language backends — llava_llama, llava_mistral, llava_mpt — each mix them into their HuggingFace base class in about a hundred lines. The builder selects among them by substring match on the model name, and handles the awkward real-world layouts too: projector-only checkpoints that need a base model plus mm_projector.bin, unmerged LoRA adapters that are restored with non_lora_trainables.bin and merged on load, and 4-bit nf4 quantization through bitsandbytes with double quantization enabled.

The vision group rewards close reading too. clip_encoder.py wraps CLIPVisionModel in a class that never lets gradients through, selects the second-to-last hidden state, and drops the class token to keep patch features only. Its sibling CLIPVisionTowerS2 adds the scales-on-scales trick — running the tower at 336, 672, and 1008 pixels and merging — which improves the tower without touching the rest of the model. On the preprocessing side, mm_utils.py implements the anyres scheme: select_best_resolution scores candidate canvas sizes by effective versus wasted resolution, the image is divided into patches plus one global view, and unpad_image trims padding rows before the grid is flattened so wide and tall photos keep their true aspect ratio.

The training group is where the recipe becomes code. train.py holds five separate preprocess functions — one per conversation template — and LazySupervisedDataset, which defers tokenization until each sample is actually fetched and exposes modality_lengths for the grouped sampler. LLaVATrainer subclasses the HuggingFace Trainer to install that sampler, to give projector parameters their own learning rate, and to save projector-only checkpoints by gathering them out of ZeRO-3 shards. Around it sit a three-line train_mem.py entry, a FlashAttention monkey patch, and the zero3 and zero3_offload configs that the finetune script points at.

One serving file deserves its own paragraph because it quietly teaches prompt engineering internals. conversation.py is a catalog of chat templates as data: a Conversation dataclass with roles, messages, and separator styles for single-separator Vicuna, double-separator v1, LLaMA-2 instruction wrapping, MPT, and the plain format used in the first pretraining stage. The image placeholder is inserted into the first user message, and when the demo receives a picture it pads it to square with a fixed gray background color rather than cropping — the same pad choice that shows up in training as a mild hallucination reducer. Changing which template a model uses is a single conv_mode string, which is why the same weights can serve every backbone generation.

Evaluation is a fourth group worth exploring. run_llava.py is the one-call entry, model_vqa.py loops a question file against an image folder and writes answers, and the GPT-assisted review flow from the paper runs in three steps: generate answers, have GPT-4 score them against reference responses with a rule file, then summarize the verdicts into a table. Alongside sit per-benchmark evaluators — POPE, ScienceQA with its re-query variant, TextVQA — and a 301-line m4c_evaluator that parses the idiosyncratic answer formats of OCR and doc-style benchmarks. All twelve reported benchmarks are reproducible from scripts in this folder, with greedy decoding as the documented default.

From Install to First Chat

The README is blunt about platforms — Linux first, with separate docs for macOS and Windows — and the install is standard editable-package plus the training extra.

git clone https://github.com/haotian-liu/LLaVA.git
cd LLaVA
conda create -n llava python=3.10 -y
conda activate llava
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -e .
pip install -e ".[train]"
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
python -m llava.serve.cli \
    --model-path liuhaotian/llava-v1.5-7b \
    --image-file "https://llava-vl.github.io/static/images/view.jpg" \
    --load-4bit

That last command downloads the 7B checkpoint from HuggingFace, quantizes it to 4 bits, and starts an interactive terminal session about the image you passed. Swap in gradio_web_server, controller, and model_worker invocations for the full browser demo, or use the load_pretrained_model function directly in Python for the one-call quickstart, which returns the tokenizer, model, image processor, and context length in a single tuple, ready for your own inference loop.

Honest limits: this is a research repository, not a product. The README’s install section warns off non-Linux systems in bold, full fine-tuning assumes eight A100s, and the main line’s later work — LLaVA-NeXT with its 4x-pixel anyres scaling, video support, and LLaMA-3 and Qwen backbones — moved to a separate codebase, leaving this one as the 1.5-era reference. The Apache-2.0 license covers the code, while checkpoints inherit the Llama community license and the instruction data carries OpenAI terms of use. Quantized inference trades some accuracy, and the eval suite’s twelve benchmarks use greedy decoding by design rather than beam search. None of that dulls the educational value: for the smallest complete proof that an LLM can learn to see, this remains the source to read.
entry.summary: How LLaVA turns a frozen CLIP and a frozen Vicuna into a multimodal chat model with a two-layer MLP, a -200 token index, and a two-stage visual instruction tuning recipe you can read in an afternoon.

entry.title: A Neural Network With Nowhere to Hide - Inside karpathy/llm.c

link.title: A Neural Network With Nowhere to Hide - Inside karpathy/llm.c

entry.content:
Every deep learning framework makes the same bargain: you trade visibility for convenience, and after a few years you can ship models without ever seeing a training loop. llm.c, Andrej Karpathy’s follow-up to nanoGPT, tears up that bargain. It trains real GPT-2 and GPT-3 sized models in pure C and CUDA — the README’s opening line boasts that you need neither 245 MB of PyTorch nor 107 MB of CPython — and it does so under the MIT license in a repository you can read cover to cover in an afternoon. The mainline trainer is one file of 1,751 lines; the CPU reference is about a thousand more. Nothing between your data and your gradients hides behind an abstraction, and the porting energy the project unleashed says something too: the README’s forks section alone lists implementations in Rust, Zig, Go, Java, Swift, C#, Mojo, Metal, and OpenCL.

The project’s discipline is what makes it more than a stunt. Every C and CUDA path is paired with a PyTorch twin, and the two must agree: a debug-state file written by the Python side is loaded by the C tests, which compare logits, loss, and ten steps of Adam before declaring “overall okay”. The kernel library in dev/cuda starts with naive implementations and climbs to fast ones, each documented well enough to teach from, and a newer Llama 3 reference extends the same scaffolding to a modern architecture. Multi-GPU runs shard optimizer state with a ZeRO implementation in a single header, and the Makefile’s flags are the entire feature surface — precision, cuDNN attention, MPI versus NCCL. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview shows the Makefile fanning out into three trainers, the header-only components they share, and the PyTorch oracles that keep them honest.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The mainline trainer is a single 1,751-line CUDA program that reproduces GPT-2 (124M) and GPT-3 model sizes with mixed precision.
  • The CPU trainer is a pure C, fp32 reference in about one thousand readable lines — the best first file in the repo.
  • The PyTorch twin is a lightly tweaked nanoGPT whose activations must match the C code exactly.
  • The Makefile is the whole feature surface: flags for precision, cuDNN attention, and multi-GPU support.
  • The dataloader header memory-maps plain uint16 token bins, no dataset library required.
  • The matmul header wraps cuBLAS and cuBLASLt, the one place where vendor libraries are allowed to dominate.
  • The ZeRO header shards optimizer state across ranks so multi-GPU runs actually scale.
  • The kernel library collects hand-written, heavily documented kernels that climb from naive to fast.

Why You Need This

The first reason is education through subtraction. In a framework, the backward pass is a function you call; in llm.c, it is several hundred lines of explicit C that you can step through with a debugger, and the README even tells you to replace -O3 with -g and do exactly that. Reading the CPU trainer end to end teaches you where every tensor lives, when gradients flow, and what an optimizer update actually touches — knowledge that transfers back to PyTorch because you finally know what it is doing for you. Any question about the backward pass becomes a breakpoint you can actually set rather than an equation you take on faith, which is a different kind of learning. The hand-written backward pass is the real prize: backpropagation stops being a magic word and becomes ordinary calculus applied layer by layer, with the chain rule written out in plain code. The repo even ships a layernorm tutorial that builds one GPT-2 layer step by step as a gentle on-ramp.

The second reason is the verification culture. Machine learning code is famously hard to test, and this repo shows the workaround: keep a PyTorch twin, export a debug state, and make the C side prove agreement on logits, loss, and ten Adam steps before anything ships. The same pattern repeats below the trainer: dev/test holds unit tests for the dataloader and other components, the test binaries exist in fp32 and mixed-precision flavors, and the reproduction scripts tie the whole thing to published model sizes. The tests compare against saved tensors, so a kernel change that shifts one bit of the math fails loudly instead of silently degrading a week-long run. If you maintain numerical code anywhere — quantization, inference servers, training jobs — this dual-implementation habit is the single most valuable thing to steal from the project, because it converts “it seems to work” into a bit-exact comparison you can rerun any time the code changes.

The third reason is performance engineering with its receipts attached. The attention kernel file walks twelve hundred documented lines from a naive implementation to fast variants, which turns “Flash Attention is faster” from folklore into something you can watch happen. The MFU header measures model flops utilization against hardware peak so speed claims have a unit, the matmul header shows exactly where vendor libraries earn their keep, and the README states the complexity budget plainly: a two percent win that costs five hundred lines may be rejected, while making cuBLAS the default matmul backend is welcomed because it is one interpretable line and a common dependency. Between the benchmarked kernels, the measured utilization, and that stated budget, the speed story closes its loop — claims, measurements, and defaults all point the same way. Watching that trade-off enforced in code review is an education in itself.

The detail graph separates six bands: root programs, PyTorch reference, llmc components, the kernel library, data preparation, and launch scripts.

Start at the root programs. The Makefile builds all the binaries, and the include lists tell the architecture story: the mainline trainer pulls in a dozen llmc headers, while the CPU trainer needs only utilities, tokenizer, and dataloader — the same loop, no CUDA anywhere. The frozen fp32 trainer preserves an early checkpoint of the GPU code for readers who want the simpler path, the test binary exists purely to certify agreement with Python — it loads a debug state written by the PyTorch twin, runs a forward pass plus ten Adam iterations, and prints “overall okay” only when the losses match — and a profiling program alongside them keeps the speed story measurable rather than anecdotal.

The components band is where the loop gets its organs. Batches flow from the dataloader, which expects bin files with a 1,024-byte header and a stream of uint16 tokens. Vocabulary handling lives in the tokenizer header, learning-rate warmup and decay in schedulers, and generation after training in the sampler, with a logger and an outlier detector keeping long runs observable. The layer headers each pick a strategy: attention compiles to the manual kernels or cuDNN Flash Attention depending on a Make flag, layernorm fuses the residual add, GELU ships its own forward and backward kernels, and AdamW fuses the update. For multi-GPU, global norm computes cross-rank clipping and ZeRO splits the optimizer state so memory scales with the cluster instead of the model.

The remaining bands complete the ecosystem. The kernel library pairs every forward file with a backward sibling — attention backward mirrors its forward, layernorm backward at 1,390 lines is the largest in the repo — and the fused classifier merges output projection with softmax loss. The softmax kernels show the numerical trick behind stable attention, and matmul backward completes the backward set with fused bias variants. On the data side, tinyshakespeare.py downloads and tokenizes into the exact bin format the dataloader expects, with sibling scripts for larger corpora, and the starter pack script fetches model, tokenizer, debug state, and data in one shot. Launch scripts pin the hyperparameters: run_gpt2_124M.sh for one node, siblings for the 350M, 774M, and 1,558M sizes, the MPI launcher for multi-node NCCL runs, and a notebook for turning sweep logs into loss curves.

From Install to First Shakespeare

The CPU quickstart needs no GPU at all:

chmod u+x ./dev/download_starter_pack.sh
./dev/download_starter_pack.sh
make train_gpt2
OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ./train_gpt2

This fetches the GPT-2 124M weights, tokenizer, debug state, and tokenized tinyshakespeare, then finetunes for forty steps with AdamW and samples Shakespeare-flavored text as validation loss falls — the README’s sample run starts near 5.25 and ends near 3.97. The same starter pack powers the fp32 GPU path (make train_gpt2fp32cu) and the mainline mixed-precision build (make train_gpt2cu), with USE_CUDNN=1 swapping in cuDNN Flash Attention if you have the libraries installed. For a real reproduction run you point the trainer at a tokenized dataset and launch through the scripts, scaling out with mpirun -np <gpus> ./train_gpt2cu once MPI and NCCL are installed; the README even demonstrates a four-GPU learning-rate sweep driven by screen sessions, a reminder that at this level an experiment manager can be a shell loop. Reproducing GPT-2 124M end to end is the project’s own recommended introduction, with the full walkthrough pinned in its discussions.

Honest limits: this is a pretraining research codebase, not a serving stack — there is no REST API, no quantized inference, no chat surface, and its speed comparisons are hardware-dependent claims against a moving PyTorch nightly rather than guarantees. Scope is deliberately GPT-2 and GPT-3 shaped, with Llama 3 covered only on the PyTorch side so far. CUDA is the first-class citizen and AMD support lives in forks, enabling cuDNN attention costs about a minute of compile time, and the multi-node scripts assume Linux cluster tooling like slurm and MPI. None of that diminishes the point: if you have ever wanted to watch a transformer learn with nothing hidden, this repository remains the clearest window in open source.
